title: The Unfinished Song
subtitle: Lanternweald — sixth expansion pass
content:
Greg had written four lines and crossed out three.

He showed me the page without pretending it was finished.

"Something's missing," he said.

The Starwake Pier stage was empty that morning. The western boards had reopened after inspection, but the public performance area wasn't booked until the weekend. A breeze rattled the spare chairs in the storage shed. Greg had brought his repaired guitar; the scratch along the body still caught the light.

Maui followed us down the pier carrying a basket of breakfast rolls.

"Great!" he said when Greg explained the problem. "I'll give you a verse about the sea. Storms, great deeds, an enormous hero—"

"I was hoping for something smaller," Greg said.

"Small hero?"

"No hero, actually."

Maui looked personally wounded.

Greg played the four-note phrase again, the one he'd built from the ferry bell at Tideglass. The fifth note rose and settled in a way that reminded me of somebody returning after a long absence.

"See?" he said. "After that it needs a breath, but whenever I write words, I fill it up."

Maui leaned on the railing. "The problem is you're thinking too quietly. The ocean—"

"Can you just sit with me for a while?" Greg interrupted.

There was nothing angry in his voice. He looked tired.

Maui stared. "You don't need me to do anything?"

"I asked because I like having you around. You're good at looking at the water without getting bored."

"I'm also good at a lot of other things."

"I know."

The silence that followed made me want to jump in and explain both men to each other. Maui was trying to contribute; Greg wanted company. They could probably solve it themselves.

So I carried the breakfast basket to the bench and passed out the rolls.

Greg played again.

Maui lasted almost two minutes without speaking. Then he pointed toward the far end of the pier.

"That board is loose."

"It passed inspection," I said.

"It's making a sound."

Greg stopped playing. "What kind of sound?"

Maui tapped the railing once, listening. "Like the line on a boat when it starts taking weight. Not danger exactly. Just something asking to be checked."

Greg looked at his guitar. "Huh."

I knew the look. He'd found a thought he wanted to keep.

"Don't make him sing about the board," I warned.

Greg grinned. "I might."

Maui looked pleased. "Finally. A subject worthy of a song."

The three of us sat until the wind shifted. We listened to ropes clicking against cleats and water moving below the supports. The low note from the old drainage passage did not sound; Fen had recorded an ordinary tide that morning. There was no mystery demanding we stop enjoying breakfast.

After a while Greg asked Maui, "What's the sound you miss most from home?"

Maui didn't answer immediately.

Then he said, "The moment just before a wave breaks on the reef. People hear the crash. I hear the water pulling itself together."

Greg nodded and played a note without words.

Maui listened.

"That one," he said quietly.

Greg tried it again. He moved two fingers along the strings, leaving a longer gap after the fifth note.

I could see Maui wanting to fill it. He opened his mouth, closed it, and looked down at his hands.

"Do you want me to do something?" he finally asked.

"Stay," Greg said.

Maui nodded.

The answer was almost painfully simple.

Before Steven came, Tamsin walked down the safe side of the pier with a clipboard tucked beneath her arm. She heard the same faint rattle Maui had pointed out and stopped.

"Good ear," she told him. "It passed the earlier check, but this wind is different. I'll log it before the next set."

Maui looked so pleased that Greg grinned.

"See? You helped without writing me a sea-king anthem."

"I still have excellent rhymes available."

"Keep them for later."

Tamsin tested the cleat and marked the board for a second inspection before the weekend performance. It wasn't an emergency, and she didn't need the whole stage closed. The tiny distinction mattered: noticing a problem wasn't the same as declaring everything ruined, and somebody qualified had to decide what the sound meant.

Greg stopped playing until Tamsin finished. He asked whether the inspection would change his rehearsal time and offered to move to the sheltered east bench if it did. She said that would be sensible, thanked him, and went back to her work.

We carried the guitar case to the bench. Maui looked at the cleared stage.

"I thought the sound was only something to fix."

"Sometimes it's a piece of a song," Greg said. "Sometimes it's a safety problem. You can listen for both."

Maui considered that, then leaned against the railing with his breakfast roll.

I wanted to say something important about the way he was learning. Instead I asked if he wanted the last piece of bread.

"Obviously."

Greg held out his hand for it first. Maui stared at him in betrayal. They argued cheerfully over the roll until I tore it in half, which struck me as considerably better music than a speech about sharing.

Around midday Steven arrived carrying a small tin of snacks. He waved to me, hugged Greg, and asked whether he was interrupting.

"Not at all," Greg said. "We're doing complicated artistic work."

Steven looked at the three of us sitting silently.

"Looks intense."

"Very," Maui agreed.

Steven laughed and settled at the edge of the bench. He didn't ask to hear a private song before it was ready. Greg played a bit of the new melody because he wanted to, not because his son had to be an audience.

By late afternoon the song still had only two lines.

Greg looked happier.

On the walk back to Tideglass, Maui carried the empty basket. He had a strange expression, as though he'd done a difficult task and wasn't sure whether anyone had noticed.

"Did you enjoy today?" I asked.

"I was waiting for Greg to need me."

"He did."

"I didn't fix anything."

"You listened."

"Very heroic."

"Not everything is supposed to be."

He stopped beside the sea-glass garden. The raised beds were full of the tiny, surviving signs of the season. A white flower bent in the salt wind but did not break.

"Sometimes I worry," he said, "that if I'm not doing something remarkable, you won't need me."

I took his hand. "I don't want you because you're necessary. I want you because I like the person who sits beside me, even when there's nothing to rescue."

He looked down at me.

"That person says very few intelligent things."

"True."

"Terrible cook."

"Frequently."

"Excellent at carrying blankets."

"Legendary."

He laughed and drew me close enough to kiss. The kiss was gentle, a little shy, warmed by the long ordinary day.

Later Greg sent a note. He had kept the space between the notes, written one new line, and left the song unfinished.

Beneath it he added: *Tell Maui thanks for sitting with me.*

I showed Maui.

He read it twice.

Then he put the note beside the tiny wooden fish, where he kept things that made him remember the difference between being admired and being wanted.

That night he didn't tell me a heroic story.

We listened to the sea until we were ready to go inside.
